books.section: Topic 5.9 Government Policies During the Civil War

options.text: Abolitionists who had long demanded an end to slavery

options.misconception: European governments supported the Confederacy because of it.
options.text: European governments seeking to recognize the Confederacy

options.misconception: Northern Democrats who opposed action against slavery supported it.
options.text: Northern Democrats who opposed any action against slavery

rationales.A: Abolitionists had long demanded emancipation and welcomed the Proclamation, even while pressing for more. They praised the step and kept pushing for full abolition and equal rights.
rationales.B: Confederate planters opposed emancipation; they did not support it.
rationales.C: European governments did not rally to the Confederacy because of it.
rationales.D: Many Northern Democrats who opposed action against slavery criticized it.
rationales.general:
1. Ask who had demanded this. Abolitionists had long called for an end to slavery.
2. Ask how they would receive it. As a welcome step, even while pressing for more.
3. Test the opposites. Planters, pro-Confederate Europeans, and anti-emancipation Democrats all opposed it.
4. Match the supporters. The group that asked for emancipation is the group that welcomed it.
Remember: support usually comes from the people who asked for the change.

source: original; stimulus is a verbatim public-domain excerpt from the Emancipation Proclamation (1863)
stem: Which of the following groups would have been most likely to support Lincoln’s action in 1863?

stimulus.source_note: Abraham Lincoln, Emancipation Proclamation, January 1, 1863, public domain.
stimulus.text: “And by virtue of the power, and for the purpose aforesaid, I do order and declare that all persons held as slaves within said designated States, and parts of States, are, and henceforward shall be free.”
